To recruit, retain and support NHS staff while keeping care safe and high quality, the workforce plan should prioritise flexible, sustainable working patterns alongside strong wellbeing and development support. Flexible hours, part-time roles, job-sharing and phased retirement options are not concessions but essential tools to widen the staff pool, reduce burnout and keep experienced clinicians at the bedside. Practical childcare and family-friendly policies—on-site or nearby, subsidised or extended hours—make careers in the NHS compatible with family life, which in turn boosts retention. Also crucial are proactive mental health services and workload management: confidential wellbeing support, easier access to occupational health, protected time for supervision and reflection, and realistic rosters that prevent chronic fatigue. Safe staffing levels with sufficient admin and allied health support reduce pressure on clinicians and protect patient safety. Finally, robust training, clear career progression, and return-to-practice routes (including apprenticeships and CPD) keep staff engaged. Mentoring, leadership development and digital tools to cut needless admin help preserve energy for patients. In my experience, these elements together stabilise teams and improve continuity of care.

I believe the NHS workforce plan should prioritise freeing clinicians from unnecessary targets, paperwork and duplicated tasks, so they can devote more time to direct patient care while still keeping safety and high-quality standards. To achieve this, the plan should: reduce administrative burden by trimming non-essential targets and duplicative data entry; streamline referrals and care pathways so patients aren’t bounced between services; invest in interoperable, user-friendly IT systems and a single real-time booking platform to cut down on repeated data entry and missed appointments; recruit and retain staff by offering flexible working, supportive supervision and clear career development, with appropriate staffing levels so GP practices and community teams aren’t stretched; create roles that take on admin tasks (care coordinators, reception/triage staff) so clinicians can focus on assessment and treatment; and ensure ongoing training and wellbeing support that recognises workload pressures. In my experience, when IT is slow or processes aren’t aligned, clinician time vanishes on admin rather than patients. A simpler, better-supported system can improve waiting times and safety alike.

From my perspective here in Scotland, a NHS workforce plan must put people first and be practical about what helps local services work safely and well. It should prioritise recruiting and retaining a stable, well-supported workforce, backed by clear career progression, fair pay and predictable rosters. It must also recognise we now need robust digital tools, but not at the expense of those less comfortable with technology.

Invest strongly in interoperable IT: secure systems and a shared, patient-centred record across GP practices, hospitals, mental health teams and social care. This reduces duplication, speeds up referrals and protects patient safety. Staff need ongoing digital training, user-friendly systems, and adequate IT support. Importantly, keep non-digital routes for digitally excluded patients—phone triage, home visits and accessible paper records.

We should also join up funding with social care, mental health and community services to redistribute workload and deliver holistic care. Multidisciplinary teams, care coordinators, and community hubs funded across sectors would make a real difference in rural and urban areas alike. Add flexible working and strong wellbeing support to retain staff. With these actions, high-quality, safe care becomes sustainable for communities across Scotland.

Fourth, fund protected clinical supervision and reflective practice; monthly case discussions, remote options, and access to mentorship, to sustain safe care as roles evolve. Fifth, design workforce models around local demand, enabling extended hours for mental health and urgent care, with safe staffing ratios and flexible rotas. Finally, use real-time data to monitor safety outcomes and patient experience, adjusting training and staffing promptly.

From my perspective living in England and relying on GP, community health and mental health services, I think the NHS workforce plan must be built around safe, sustainable and person-centred care. I strongly support expanding and regulating multidisciplinary teams—nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and other allied roles—so that skilled professionals can share routine and non-specialist work from GPs, while ensuring every task is properly trained and supervised. This approach helps preserve continuity of care and protects quality as demand grows.

Key priorities I’d want to see in any workforce plan:

- Expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams with clear scopes of practice. This means extra training and formal supervision for roles like practice nurses taking lead on chronic disease monitoring, pharmacist-led medication reviews for people with polypharmacy, and physician associates or advanced nurse practitioners handling regular check-ins for stable conditions. In practice this has already helped in some areas by freeing GPs to focus on complex cases while still keeping patients within a familiar care network.

- Prioritise safe staffing ratios and continuity-preserving models. It’s not enough to increase headcount; you have to ensure there are enough staff with the right mix in the same practice team so patients see the same people. A named or stable care team across primary and community services reduces the need for repeating histories and supports better judgment when coordinating across services. This also means data-driven rostering to manage peak times, extended hours where appropriate, and real-time monitoring of workload to prevent burnout.

- Strengthen links with social care, mental health and community services with joint funding and governance. A joined-up approach means teams can share records, co-design care plans, and redistribute tasks where appropriate—without compromising safety. For example, co-locating district nurses with mental health staff or social workers in a single hub enables timely home-based support, reducing hospital admissions and improving overall wellbeing.

- Invest in training, supervision and professional development. Create clear pathways for career progression within primary care teams, with protected time for CPD, supervision, and reflective practice. This helps staff stay motivated and reduces turnover. Practical supports like mentorship schemes and return-to-practice routes will also help fill gaps more quickly.

- Implement safety monitoring and governance that keeps quality high. Regular audits, near-miss reporting, and dashboards that track patient outcomes, wait times, and staff wellbeing are essential. The plan should specify acceptable patient safety standards for each role and set expectations for ongoing evaluation of how new team-based models affect care quality.

- Recruitment, retention and wellbeing incentives. To sustain a diverse, skilled workforce, the plan should include targeted recruitment for underserved areas, flexible working patterns, and support for staff mental health and wellbeing. Recognising and rewarding teams for effective collaboration and improved patient outcomes will also help retain staff long term.

Concrete examples from my experience reinforce these points. In another area, a district nurse and community mental health clinician collaborate on home-based support; coordination of care plans reduces avoidable crises and hospital visits. These models show how the right team mix, well-supported supervision, and strong cross-service links can deliver safer, higher-quality care while improving patients’ experience of continuity.

To sum up, the workforce plan should prioritise expanding and regulating multidisciplinary teams, ensuring safe staffing and continuity, strengthening cross-sector collaboration with joint funding and governance, and embedding robust safety and wellbeing supports. When done well, this approach not only maintains but enhances clinical quality and patient experience, by spreading appropriate workload across skilled professionals and keeping patients in familiar, coherent care networks.

From living in rural Wales, I’ve seen how fragile arrangements can become when staffing is thin and admin piles up. A workforce plan that truly supports recruitment, retention and safe, high-quality care needs to be grounded in local data and practical, predictable systems. I’d prioritise the following, with examples drawn from everyday experience in our communities.

- Localised data, modelling and evaluation. Develop transparent, localised workforce data, alongside clear modelling and KPIs that reflect real community needs. This should feed into funding decisions and performance monitoring, not sit in a spreadsheet drawer. For example, a dashboard that tracks GP, district nurse, mental health professional and physio staffing by locality, plus wait times for same-day access and to see a clinician, would make it possible to spot gaps early and target training or flexible staffing pools. Tie these metrics to concrete evaluation frameworks so we can see what works in practice and adjust quickly.

- Clear scope-of-practice, revalidation and safe supervision. In rural areas, expanding capable roles can be essential to bridge gaps, but it must be underpinned by clear agreements on scope-of-practice, revalidation, and indemnity. Fund protected clinical supervision for new roles—such as advanced clinical practitioners, nurse prescribers and allied health assistants—so they can work confidently while patient safety is maintained. For us, this would mean guaranteed supervision slots, perhaps via a regional virtual hub, and predictable indemnity terms that don’t deter clinicians from taking on innovative roles in remote communities.

- Reducing unnecessary targets, paperwork and duplication. Clinicians in small communities often wear many hats and spend too much time on admin that could be streamlined. A plan should simplify referrals, consolidate multiple data entry points, and improve IT usability. Real-world example: a single, user-friendly electronic record with integrated, easy-to-access referral pathways to community services and secondary care. Better IT support and clearer processes would reclaim significant time for patient-facing care and reduce frustration that drives burnout.

- Flexible, locally deployable workforce models. Co-locate services where possible and support mobile or outreach teams that can visit villages on planned schedules. This would complement telehealth hubs and help patients in remote areas access GPs, mental health support and rehabilitation without long journeys. Flexible contracts, local training pipelines and attractive retention packages (housing support, relocation, and family-friendly terms) should be offered to encourage clinicians to work in rural settings for defined periods.

- Training, career progression and partnerships with Welsh universities. Build longer-term pipelines by strengthening rural training placements and clear pathways from student to frontline clinician in community settings. This includes GP training posts linked with local health boards, nursing roles with prescriber options, and collaborative schemes with universities to grow the workforce locally rather than relying on out-of-area recruitment.

- Safeguards to maintain safety and quality. Any plan must ensure safe staffing levels, reasonable working hours, and mental health and wellbeing support for staff. In small communities, a crisis can overwhelm the system quickly; robust rotas, cover arrangements and a reliable locum pool can keep services stable without compromising care quality.

- Clear accountability and community involvement. Let local communities have a say in how staffing meets their needs, with transparent reporting on capacity, wait times and service delivery. If people can see that the plan is working in practice—and that it adapts when it isn’t—trust in the NHS strengthens and staff feel valued.

In practice, a well-rounded NHS workforce plan for Wales would blend data-driven decision making with practical supports for those delivering care in rural areas. It should free clinicians from avoidable admin, empower new roles with solid supervision and indemnity, and create flexible, locally attuned service models that keep patients safe and cared for close to home. If these elements are in place, we can expect fewer delays, steadier access to mental health and primary care, and a more sustainable rural workforce that remains motivated to serve their communities.

From my perspective living in England and juggling family life with work, the NHS workforce plan must be concrete, locally informed and people-centred. It should prioritise three things: transparent, localised data and evaluation; expanded and well-supported multidisciplinary teams; and safe staffing that protects quality as access improves. When those pieces align, we can recruit, keep and support staff while still delivering high‑quality care.

First, we need transparent local data, robust modelling and clear KPIs, linked to real-world funding and performance review. Practice and system planners should have access to real-time dashboards that show vacancy rates, turnover, training uptake, sickness absence, wait times, first-contact resolution, and patient safety indicators. Importantly, these metrics must feed into evaluation frameworks that assess whether changes are delivering better access without eroding care quality. In practice, this means local authorities and NHS bodies sharing consistent data at neighbourhood and practice levels, so early warning signals (for example, rising wait times in primary care or increasing inappropriate GP referrals) trigger targeted support. Local modelling should test different workforce mixes before money is released—for instance, how many nurse prescribers, pharmacists, PAs, or paramedics are needed to safely manage routine care while GPs focus on complex cases. In our area, even a modest shift—embedding a practice pharmacist and a physiotherapist into the team—helped clear backlogs and speed up appropriate care, illustrating how data-driven decisions can reallocate tasks safely and effectively.

Second, expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams with proper training and supervision to redistribute GP workload without compromising safety. The reform here isn’t about more bodies; it’s about the right mix of skilled professionals who can triage, treat routine issues, and support GPs with complex cases. Nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and allied health professionals should work to the top of their competence, with clear scopes of practice and accessible supervision. In a practical sense, that means funded training pipelines for clinical fellows, pharmacist prescribers, physiotherapists and PAs, plus protected time for ongoing professional development and reflective support. A local pilot where pharmacists and physiotherapists join the team showed how routine musculoskeletal care could be managed outside GP appointments, freeing GPs to focus on more complex needs and reducing unnecessary referrals. Similarly, nurse practitioners in our practice were able to assess a persistent skin issue promptly, illustrating how tiered teams can deliver safer, faster care. Regular clinical governance and peer review should accompany expanded roles to maintain high standards and patient safety.

Third, prioritise safe staffing ratios, continuity-preserving models and ongoing safety monitoring. As access improves, we must ensure we don’t simply push more patients through the door with limited attention to staffing safety. Safe ratios for nurses and frontline staff are essential to prevent burnout, maintain quality of care, and sustain recruitment. Continuity matters too: stable teams and predictable rosters help patients build trust, reduce handoffs, and lower the risk of errors. This means deliberate workforce planning that avoids over‑reliance on temporary staffing, supports long‑term career pathways, and includes mental health and wellbeing resources for clinicians. Safety monitoring should be built into every reform: incident reporting, near-miss analysis, and patient outcomes must be part of the evaluation framework so we can adjust quickly if a new model threatens care quality.

To knit these elements together, funding needs to be flexible and outcomes‑driven. Localised workforce data should inform where to invest in training, recruitment, and expanded MDTs. Clear governance should accompany new team configurations, ensuring transparent supervision structures and safe delegation of tasks. In my experience, when teams are well-supported, patients experience shorter waits for routine care, while GPs retain capacity to manage complex cases and hospital liaison becomes smoother.

In summary, an NHS workforce plan that truly supports staff and maintains high-quality care should be grounded in local data and evaluation, expand multidisciplinary teams with robust training and supervision, and insist on safe staffing and continuous safety monitoring. When implemented with these priorities, we can improve timely access without compromising safety or patient outcomes, and we can also create a more sustainable, fulfilling workplace for clinicians across primary and community care.

From my perspective living in England and juggling family needs, I think any NHS workforce plan that aims to recruit, retain and support staff while keeping care safe must do two core things at once: expand capable, well-supported teams beyond doctors, and cut the non-clinical clutter that eats into real patient time. These arrangements can trim waiting times and keep patients out of the GP queue for matters that don’t require a doctor’s input. Second, reduce unnecessary targets, paperwork and duplicated tasks, while streamlining referrals and improving IT usability to free clinician time for patient-facing care. If designed with careful training, clear governance, and a patient-centred emphasis, a broadened, well-supported team-based model could deliver safer, higher-quality care while addressing the practical realities families face day-to-day.

A workforce plan for the NHS should be pragmatic, locally accountable and focused on patient safety above all. - Provide a clearly funded career ladder with protected CPD time. Clinicians—whether GPs, nurses, or allied health professionals—should know what progress looks like, how to access training, and how to move into leadership or specialist roles without losing financial security.
- Invest in mentorship and return-to-practice schemes. This would help people rejoin after a break for family, caring responsibilities, or burnout, and would also ease the transition for early-career staff who need support as they gain confidence.
- Create structured, funded support for ongoing professional development (CPD) and supervision, with protected time and access to high-quality teaching. The goal is to reduce burnout by making it feasible to grow skills without being overwhelmed by workload.
- Build support for flexible working and succession planning. To retain talented staff, we need teams that can share workloads and cover for absences without compromising patient safety.

Invest in interoperable IT while safeguarding alternatives
- Modernise IT with interoperable, secure systems that actually reduce friction in day-to-day work. Staff should be trained to use digital tools confidently, and systems must be designed around patient safety first, not just data collection.
- Ensure robust digital training and ongoing support, but also safeguard non-digital routes for patients who are digitally excluded. In practice, that means clear phone lines, simple booking processes, and staff who can help people through both digital and non-digital channels.
- Build digital champions in practices who can assist colleagues and patients alike, and ensure IT rollouts include real-time feedback from frontline teams so problems are fixed quickly.

Protect safe, high-quality care in every setting
- Emphasise safe staffing levels and reducing avoidable burnout. Adequate staffing isn’t a luxury; it’s a patient safety issue.
- Encourage cross-skilling and team-based care so, for example, nurses and healthcare assistants can manage routine tasks, freeing GPs to handle complex cases. This must be paired with strong supervision and clear accountability.
- Prioritise return-to-practice pathways for clinicians who paused their careers due to health or caregiving responsibilities, ensuring they receive up-to-date training and support to re-enter safely.

Accountability, equity and local delivery
- Establish transparent targets for recruitment, retention and progression by service type and geography, with independent reporting on equity (age, disability, income, rurality). If targets aren’t met, there should be corrective action, not excuses.
- Align workforce planning with local health and social care needs, ensuring community and primary care services aren’t neglected as digital tools expand.
- Incentivise partnerships with local schools, colleges and communities to advertise career paths and create locally rooted incentives to stay in Northern Ireland.

In short, a successful NHS workforce plan must grow our own clinicians, support them with protected development and clear career paths, invest in secure, user-friendly IT while guaranteeing non-digital access, and keep patient safety at the centre of staffing decisions. Only then can we deliver high-quality care that adapts to digital advances without leaving anyone behind, especially in rural communities where access and continuity of care are most at stake.

A plan that is serious about safety will specify minimum staffing levels for different times of day and different services, plus contingency options when gaps arise.

The aim isn’t to dilute expertise but to distribute workload safely so patients get timely access without compromising safety.

Second, make local data and evaluation the backbone of planning. A one-size-fits-all plan won’t work because population needs, geography and practice size vary. What we need is transparent, locally driven data on skill mix, vacancy rates, staff turnover, caseloads, and demand patterns. Accompanying KPIs should cover access (time to first contact, same-day responses), safety (prescribing error rates, adverse events, avoidable hospitalisations), clinical quality (outcome measures for chronic conditions), workforce health (staff burnout indicators, sickness absence), and patient experience.

Evaluation frameworks must be built in from the start: plan-do-study-act cycles, real-world pilots with independent evaluation, and a clear route for learning and scaling where results are positive. Local authorities and clinical commissioning groups should publish findings and adjust funding and training accordingly. It’s important that data be used to inform decisions about where to expand roles and where to invest in additional supervision or infrastructure—never to justify a reduction in professional oversight or patient contact.

In practice, I’ve seen the benefits when teams in some practices include nurse practitioners and pharmacists working closely with GPs; appointment availability improves, and patients with stable conditions enjoy more efficient, safer care. My worry is that without a rigorous data- and governance-first approach, expanding roles could simply shift the bottleneck elsewhere or erode continuity of care.

So, in short: prioritise expanding and regulating multidisciplinary teams with robust training, supervision, and governance; couple that with transparent local data, solid modelling, and clear, outcome-focused KPIs and evaluation. Do it with protected time and funding for learning, ensure strong patient safety nets, and keep digital tools as a complement—not a replacement—for human, local decision-making. If done thoughtfully, this could deliver faster access and safer care across GP, community health and mental health services; if rushed or under-supported, it risks unequal access and variability in quality.

Clinicians reported lower burnout, better morale, and a steadier level of care for patients. Patients benefited too, with more predictable access and less churn in their care team.
